newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Labour, Alliance plan talks on confidence.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Labour, Alliance plan talks on confidence.

text.p: Representatives from the centre-left Labour Party and the five party left-wing Alliance grouping will hold further informal talks on Thursday aimed at setting the basis for Alliance support for a centre-left government, their leaders said.

Nationalist NZ First holds the balance of power after the October 12 election and is negotiating separately with both the conservative incumbent National Party and Labour over the shape of the next government.
If NZ First opts to join National the two would have an outright majority with 61 seats in the 120 seat single chamber parliament.
But a Labour-NZ First government would have a combined 54 seats and would need the support of the Alliance's 13 MPs to be certain of a majority.
Negotiating teams from Labour and the Alliance met for two hours on Wednesday, with talks centring on confidence votes, Labour leader Helen Clark said.

"Obviously the number one issue is confidence. The Alliance has repeated its position that in general terms if the agreement for a Labour-NZ First government moves in the direction of the policy they have signalled it is likely to be a goer, but obviously we have to have further discussions down the track," Clark said.

She said Labour was not seeking a "blank cheque" of support from the Alliance. She indicated Labour would take a narrow view of issues that should be confidence votes and not use them to force through votes it would not otherwise win.
The Alliance has drafted a definition of confidence and what it would mean for a minority government and the party supporting that government, for Labour to respond to.

A government must show it has the confidence of most MPs in Parliament to rule. A single lost confidence vote does not require a government to resign automatically, but it would lead to careful scrutiny of whether a government could continue.
NZ First is expected to indicate next week whether National or Labour is its preferred coalition partner.
Clark said she felt talks with the Alliance had indicated the basis existed for a Labour-NZ First government to function well.
Alliance leader Jim Anderton said the talks with Labour had been very positive.
"The Alliance has stood to play a constructive and positive role in forming a new alternative government to National and these talks should take us on that path," Anderton said.
He said he expected to speak with NZ First leader Winston Peters about the basis of Alliance support for a centre-left coalition.
Asked how Peters should view the Labour-Alliance meeting, Clark said: "I hope he will take enormous heart from it."
Asked what message National caretaker Prime Minister Jim Bolger should take from the meeting, Clark said: "Terror."
Parliament must meet no later than December 13, but is likely to open on December 10.
